goal: What evidence shows that autonomous research agents outperform a single well-prompted model on difficult technical research tasks?

text: A multi-agent research system substantially outperforms a single agent using the same frontier model on an internal breadth-heavy research evaluation (Anthropic reports ~90% improvement).
Agentic deep-research systems score far higher than the same vendor's single non-agentic models on hard public benchmarks such as Humanity's Last Exam and BrowseComp.
Most of the measured advantage of research agents is explained by extra compute/token spend and tool access rather than by agent architecture per se; equal-budget comparisons are rarely reported.
When cost is controlled, simple baselines (single model with retries/sampling) can match or beat complex agent systems on some benchmarks.
On long-horizon difficult research-engineering tasks, autonomous agents still underperform skilled humans given larger time budgets, limiting claims of autonomous superiority.
Multi-agent LLM systems often show only minimal gains over single-agent baselines and fail in systematic ways.

result: BrowseComp: Deep Research 5.2x o1 (+41.6 pts), 27x GPT-4o w/ browsing; HLE: 2.05x o3-mini-high (+13.6 pts). Anthropic: multi-agent uses ~3.75x the tokens of a single agent (15x vs 4x of chat) for a reported 1.90x eval gain - gains not compute-matched.
